posts.title: Githug OAuth Flow with C#
posts.html:
Understanding GitHub OAuth Authorization Code Flow with C#

OAuth 2.0 is the industry-standard protocol for authorization. When integrating with GitHub, the Authorization Code Flow is the most common OAuth 2.0 flow, designed primarily for web applications running on a server. This flow ensures secure communication between your application and GitHub, as it involves exchanging tokens only on the server side. Let’s dive into how to implement this flow using C#.

Types of OAuth Flows Supported by GitHub

Before diving deeper into the Authorization Code Flow, it's essential to understand the different OAuth flows GitHub supports:

  1. Authorization Code Flow: This is the most common flow, used by server-side applications. It provides the highest level of security since the exchange of the authorization code for an access token happens on the server side.

  2. Implicit Flow: Used primarily by client-side applications, such as single-page applications (SPAs). It allows the client to obtain an access token directly, without needing to handle the authorization code. This flow is less secure because the access token is exposed to the client.

  3. Device Flow: Designed for devices that lack a web browser or have limited input capabilities, like smart TVs or command-line tools. This flow involves the user authorizing the application on a separate device.

  4. Client Credentials Flow: Suitable for machine-to-machine communication, where the application itself acts on its own behalf, rather than on behalf of a user. This flow is often used for backend services or applications that don’t require user interaction.

  5. GitHub Apps Flow: This flow is tailored for GitHub Apps, allowing them to interact with repositories and organizations with specific permissions and more granular control over access.

Each of these flows serves a specific use case, but the Authorization Code Flow is the most widely used for traditional web applications. Now that we’ve covered the different flows, let's explore how to implement the Authorization Code Flow in a C# application.

Setting Up Your GitHub OAuth Application

Before writing any code, you must register your application on GitHub to obtain the necessary credentials. Go to your GitHub settings, navigate to "Developer settings" and then to "OAuth Apps." Click on "New OAuth App" and fill in the required details. The critical pieces of information here are the Client ID and Client Secret, which your application will use to authenticate with GitHub.

Building the Authorization URL

The first step in the Authorization Code Flow is to redirect the user to GitHub's authorization server. This step will prompt the user to log in (if they haven’t already) and grant your application the required permissions.

In C#, you can construct the authorization URL like this:

var clientId = "your_client_id"; // Replace with your Client ID
var redirectUri = "https://yourapp.com/callback"; // Replace with your Redirect URI
var scope = "user repo"; // Scopes determine the level of access your app is requesting
var state = Guid.NewGuid().ToString(); // State helps to protect against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks

var authorizationUrl = $"https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id={clientId}&redirect_uri={redirectUri}&scope={scope}&state={state}";

// Redirect the user to GitHub's OAuth login page
Response.Redirect(authorizationUrl);

When the user visits this URL, they will be asked to log in and authorize your application to access their GitHub account. If they approve, GitHub will redirect them back to your redirectUri with an authorization code.

Handling the Callback and Exchanging the Authorization Code

Once GitHub redirects back to your application with an authorization code, the next step is to exchange this code for an access token. This is done via a POST request to GitHub's token endpoint.

Here’s how you can handle the callback and perform the token exchange:

[HttpGet]
public async Task<IActionResult> Callback(string code, string state)
{
    var clientId = "your_client_id";
    var clientSecret = "your_client_secret";

    using (var httpClient = new HttpClient())
    {
        var tokenRequest = new Dictionary<string, string>
        {
            { "client_id", clientId },
            { "client_secret", clientSecret },
            { "code", code }
        };

        var requestContent = new FormUrlEncodedContent(tokenRequest);
        var response = await httpClient.PostAsync("https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token", requestContent);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var responseContent = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        var queryParams = HttpUtility.ParseQueryString(responseContent);
        var accessToken = queryParams["access_token"];

        // Use the access token to interact with GitHub's API
        return Ok(accessToken);
    }
}

The code parameter is provided by GitHub in the callback URL after the user approves the authorization. You send this code, along with your client credentials, to GitHub’s token endpoint. If successful, GitHub will return an access token that your application can use to interact with GitHub’s API on behalf of the user.

Making Authenticated API Requests

With the access token in hand, you can now make authenticated requests to GitHub’s API. The access token should be included in the Authorization header of your HTTP requests.

Here’s an example of how to fetch the authenticated user's GitHub profile:

public async Task<IActionResult> GetUserProfile(string accessToken)
{
    using (var httpClient = new HttpClient())
    {
        httpClient.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", accessToken);

        var response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://api.github.com/user");

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
        var content = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();

        return Ok(content);
    }
}

In this example, the Authorization header is set to include the access token, allowing you to retrieve the user's profile information. You can use the same approach to access other GitHub API endpoints, depending on the scopes granted during the authorization process.

Refreshing the Access Token (Optional)

Although GitHub’s access tokens do not expire by default, if you request tokens with a limited lifetime or anticipate token revocation, you may need to implement token refreshing. GitHub does not support the OAuth 2.0 Refresh Token flow natively, so you would typically need to prompt the user to reauthorize the application if the token is no longer valid.

Conclusion

The OAuth Authorization Code Flow is a powerful and secure method for authorizing web applications to interact with GitHub on behalf of a user. By following the steps outlined in this guide, you can integrate GitHub authentication into your C# application, enabling seamless and secure access to GitHub's APIs. Whether you're building a tool for developers, automating workflows, or integrating with GitHub in other ways, OAuth provides the foundation for secure, user-consented API access.

posts.title: Publish C# Project to Nuget.org
posts.html:
Using NuGet packages and nuget.org are a great way to share our .NET projects with other developers and also distribute your code across multiple projects.

In this guide, we'll walk through the process of publishing an existing .NET project as a NuGet package on NuGet.org. Let's use the Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles project as an example, which is hosted on GitHub.

Prepare the Project for Packaging

Let's start by cloning the project or using DevContainers to edit in Github Cloud (as demonstrated here Create and Configure a GitHub Codespace

# clones the project 
> git clone https://github.com/ricardodemauro/Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles.git
> cd Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles

Open the Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.Env.csproj file and include the necessary NuGet package metadata.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
 <PropertyGroup>
   <TargetFramework>netstandard2.0</TargetFramework>
     
   <!--Starts here-->
   <PackageId>Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles</PackageId>
   <PackageVersion>1.0.0</Version>
   <Authors>Ricardo Mauro</Authors>
   <Description>Extension to read .env files in dotnet core projects</Description>
   <RepositoryUrl>https://github.com/ricardodemauro/Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles.git</RepositoryUrl>
     
    <PackageIconUrl>rmauro-favico-32.png</PackageIconUrl>
    <PackageIcon>rmauro-favico-32.png</PackageIcon>

  • Follow the prompts to complete your registration, including email verification.

Click "Create" to generate a new API key.

Provide a name for your key (e.g., "MyAwesomeLibrary Publishing Key").

Choose the scope for the key:

  • "Push new packages and package versions" if you're only publishing.
  • "Push and unlist packages" if you also want the ability to unlist packages.

Select the glob pattern for the packages this key can push. Use * for all packages or specify package names. Then click "Create".

Copy the generated API Key.

  1. Use the following command to publish your package, replacing your_api_key with your actual API key:
> dotnet nuget push `
  bin/Release/Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles.1.0.0.nupkg `
  --api-key your_api_key `
  --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json

NuGet.org will process our package. It usually takes a few minutes to be available.

Here is our package: https://www.nuget.org/packages/Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.Env/

Updating Your Package

When you make changes to your project and want increment the published version.

  1. Build using the /p:Version=0.0.0.2 parameter or simply increment the <Version> number in your .csproj file
  2. Repackage and publish again
> dotnet build -c Release /p:Version=0.0.0.2

> dotnet pack --configuration Release

> dotnet nuget push `
  bin/Release/Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles.0.0.2.nupkg `
  --api-key {NUGET_API_KEY} `
  --source https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json

Best Practices for Maintaining Your NuGet Package

  • Create/Update the README.md file in the nuget.org website
  • Use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) to communicate the nature of updates
  • Regularly check for and update any dependencies in your project
  • Keep your code updated and secure against know treats
  • Rotate your API keys periodically for security

Conclusion

Publishing your existing .NET project as a NuGet package is a great way to share your work with the broader .NET community.

By following these steps, you've made your Rmauro.Extensions.Configuration.EnvFiles library easily accessible to other developers.

posts.title: Getting Started with Tmux on Terminal
posts.html:
Tmux is a terminal multiplexer that allows you to run multiple terminal sessions within a single window. It is a powerful tool for anyone who spends significant time in the terminal, offering persistent sessions, multiple panes, and flexible session management. In this guide, we will cover how to install tmux, its basic and advanced commands, and provide references for further learning.

Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. Installing Tmux Using apt
  3. Basic Tmux Commands
  4. Advanced Tmux Commands
  5. References
  6. Conclusion

Installing Tmux

Installing tmux on a Debian-based system (like Ubuntu) or WSL Terminal is straightforward using the apt package manager.

Before installing tmux, ensure your package list is up to date.

sudo apt update

Then install tmux by running.

sudo apt install tmux

You can verify the installation by checking the version.

# upper case V
tmux -V

Basic Tmux Commands

Once tmux is installed, you can start exploring its basic features.

# starting a New Session
> tmux

# detaching from a Session
Ctrl+b, then d

# reattaching to a Session
> tmux attach

# creating a New Window
  Ctrl+b, then c
  
# switching Between Windows
Ctrl+b, then n (for next window)
Ctrl+b, then p (for previous window)

Advanced Tmux Commands

Tmux's advanced features allow for more efficient and complex workflows.

# splitting Panes Horizontally
Ctrl+b, then "

# splitting Panes Vertically
Ctrl+b, then %

# resizing Panes
Ctrl+b, then arrow keys

# renaming a Session
> tmux rename-session -t [old-name] [new-name]
  
# list All Sessions
> tmux ls

# killing a Session
> tmux kill-session -t [session-name]

Cheatsheet

References

For more detailed information and advanced configurations, visit the official tmux page:

  • Tmux Official Documentation

Conclusion

Tmux is an essential tool for anyone who works extensively in the terminal. From managing multiple sessions to splitting your terminal into panes, tmux provides the flexibility and efficiency needed for a productive command-line experience.

Happy Coding

posts.title: Implicit Using in C#
posts.html:
Introduction

C# 10 introduced implicit usings, a feature designed to reduce boilerplate code by automatically including commonly used namespaces in your projects. This helps make your code cleaner and easier to manage. In this article, we'll explore what implicit usings are, how they work, how to manage them, and the benefits they offer.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Implicit Usings
  • How Implicit Usings Works
  • Enabling Implicit Usings
  • Adding Usings to Implicit Usings

What Are Implicit Usings

Implicit usings automatically include a predefined list of using directives in your C# files, so you don't need to manually add them.

This feature is enabled by default in .NET 6 or later and varies depending on the project type.

For example, in a typical .NET console application, you might have several using statements at the top of your files, like using System;, using System.Collections.Generic;, etc. With implicit usings, these are automatically included, allowing you to focus more on your code.

How Implicit Usings Works

When you create a new .NET project in .NET 6 or later, implicit usings are enabled by default. The specific namespaces included depend on the project type.

For Console Application

using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.IO;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

For ASP.NET Core Applications

/*In addition to all Console App usings*/

using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

For Worker

/*In addition to all Console App usings*/

using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging;

Enabling Implicit Usings

You can manage implicit usings through the .csproj file. This allows you to enable, disable, or customize the list of implicit usings according to your project's needs.

PS.: Implicit usings are enabled by default.

<PropertyGroup>
  <ImplicitUsings>disable</ImplicitUsings>
</PropertyGroup>

To re-enable.

<PropertyGroup>
  <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
</PropertyGroup>

Adding Usings to Implicit Usings

You can add or remove namespaces from the implicit usings list using the <Using> element in the .csproj file.

To add a custom namespace:

<ItemGroup>
  <Using Include="MyCustomNamespace" />
</ItemGroup>

To exclude a namespace:

<ItemGroup>
  <Using Remove="System.Linq" />
</ItemGroup>

Conclusion

By automatically managing common namespaces, they allow you to write cleaner, more efficient code.

Whether you use them as-is or customize them, understanding implicit usings can significantly improve your C# development experience.

Happy Coding!

Implicit usings automatically include a predefined list of `using` directives in your C# files, so you don't need to manually add them.

posts.title: Recreating AutoMapper for Speed: Manual Assignment vs. Reflection and Beyond
posts.html:
In high-performance applications, the speed at which you can map objects can make a significant difference. While AutoMapper is a popular choice for its ease of use, it may not always be the fastest option, especially when dealing with large datasets or performance-critical scenarios. In this article, we will explore various approaches to building a blazing-fast AutoMapper by leveraging everything from manual assignments to runtime-generated IL code. We'll start with the most basic—and fastest—approach, manual assignment, and then progressively optimize the process using reflection, compiled code, and more advanced techniques.

Whether you're optimizing an existing application or starting a new project, understanding the trade-offs between different mapping strategies can help you make more informed decisions. Let's dive into the world of object mapping in C# and see how each method stacks up in terms of performance.

Table of Contents

  1. Using Manual Assignments: The Baseline

Before We Start

Before we get started here’s what you’ll need.

  • Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code: You can use either of these IDEs for coding and running the examples.

  • .NET 8 SDK: Ensure that you have .NET 8 installed.

  • Console Application: We will use a console application to run the examples and benchmarks.

The Folder Structure

Inside your console application project, create the following folder structure to organize your code:

ObjectMappers/
├── Extensions.cs
├── Program.cs
└── Mappers/
    └── MapperBase.cs

/*Extensions.cs*/

using System.Reflection;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

namespace Rmauro.Optimizations.ObjectMappers;

public record struct PropertyMap(
    PropertyInfo SourceProperty, 
    PropertyInfo TargetProperty);

public class RandomModel
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string CustomerName { get; set; }

    public string DeliveryAddress { get; set; }

    public DateTime EstimatedDeliveryDate { get; set; }

    public string OrderReference { get; set; }
}

public static class ObjectExtensions
{
    [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.MethodImpl(System.Runtime.CompilerServices.MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)]
    public static IList<PropertyMap> GetMatchingProps(this object source, object target)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(target);

        var sourceProperties = source.GetType().GetProperties();
        var targetProperties = target.GetType().GetProperties();

        var properties = (from s in sourceProperties
                          from t in targetProperties
                          where s.Name == t.Name &&
                              s.CanRead &&
                              t.CanWrite &&
                              s.PropertyType.IsPublic &&
                              t.PropertyType.IsPublic &&
                              s.PropertyType == t.PropertyType &&
                              (
                                  (s.PropertyType.IsValueType && t.PropertyType.IsValueType) 
                                  || 
                                  (s.PropertyType == typeof(string) && t.PropertyType == typeof(string))
                              )
                          select new PropertyMap
                          {
                              SourceProperty = s,
                              TargetProperty = t
                          }).ToList();

        return properties;
    }
}

The other files needed for the different mapping approaches will be created as we progress through the article. By the end, you’ll have a fully functional project that demonstrates each method's performance.

1. Using Manual Assignment (Baseline)

Manual assignment is the most straightforward and fastest approach for mapping objects. By directly assigning values from one object to another, you avoid any runtime overhead, making this method the most efficient in terms of performance.

The most boring one!!!

This approach serves as our baseline for comparison:

public Destination Map(Source source)
{
    return new Destination
    {
        Property1 = source.Property1,
        Property2 = source.Property2,
        // Continue for all properties...
    };
}

2. Using Reflection (Not Optimized)

Reflection allows you to inspect and manipulate objects at runtime. However, this flexibility comes at a significant cost in performance due to the overhead of dynamically accessing object members.

This method is much slower than manual assignment:

public T Map<T>(object source) where T : new()
{
    var destination = new T();
    var sourceProperties = source.GetType().GetProperties();
    var destinationProperties = typeof(T).GetProperties();

    foreach (var sourceProperty in sourceProperties)
    {
        var destinationProperty = destinationProperties.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Name == sourceProperty.Name);
        if (destinationProperty != null)
        {
            destinationProperty.SetValue(destination, sourceProperty.GetValue(source));
        }
    }

    return destination;
}

3. Using Optimized Reflection

Optimized reflection attempts to reduce the overhead by caching property information or minimizing repeated lookups. Although it offers a performance improvement over basic reflection, it is still slower than manual assignment.

4. Using C# Compiled Code

A significant improvement over reflection-based mappers is to use C# compiled code. By generating and compiling mapping code at runtime, you eliminate the overhead associated with reflection, bringing the performance closer to manual assignment.

5. Using IL Runtime Generated Code

Generating Intermediate Language (IL) code at runtime allows for even finer control and further optimizations. IL generation can achieve performance that rivals or exceeds compiled C# code, making it one of the fastest approaches after manual assignment.

Measuring Performance

To accurately compare the performance of these approaches, we use the Stopwatch class in .NET. Each method is executed in a loop of 1,000,000 iterations, and the time taken is recorded.

Here's the performance measurement setup:

var stopwatch = new Stopwatch();

stopwatch.Start();

// Execute the mapping logic here 1,000,000 times

stopwatch.Stop();
Console.WriteLine($"Time elapsed: {stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms");

By using the manual assignment method as a baseline, we can clearly see how the other approaches compare in terms of speed.

Conclusion

Recreating a fast AutoMapper requires balancing performance and flexibility. While manual assignment is the fastest method, other approaches like compiled code and IL generation offer performance close to the baseline with added flexibility. Reflection-based methods, even when optimized, still lag behind due to their inherent overhead. Use this analysis to choose the method that best fits your application's performance needs.

Feel free to add the source code and performance comparisons to provide real-world data on the impact of each approach. This will help in making an informed decision based on your specific use case.

posts.title: First Look at Semantic Kernel Agents Powered by AI Assistants - PART I
posts.html:
Welcome to the first part of our series on Semantic Kernel, a powerful C# framework for building AI agents. In this article, we'll take our first steps with Semantic Kernel by creating a simple project to help you get started.

This series will guide you through the basics and gradually explore more advanced features, setting you up to build your own AI-driven applications

Series

  • Getting Started with Semantic Kernel

What is Microsoft Semantic Kernel?

Microsoft's Semantic Kernel serves primarily as an AI orchestration framework that connects your application with multiple AI model APIs. It enhances the capability of any app by enabling it to process natural language, generate insightful responses, and perform a variety of intelligent tasks.

In Microsoft words:

Semantic Kernel is an SDK that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) like OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and Hugging Face with conventional programming languages like C#, Python, and Java. Semantic Kernel achieves this by allowing you to define plugins that can be chained together in just a few lines of code.

The major components of the Semantic Kernel include:

  • Kernel Creation: The core part where you set up configurations for the AI model.
  • Function Definition: Define what the AI should accomplish (e.g., summarizing text).
  • Invoke Functions: Execute the defined functions with the required input.

Getting Started with Semantic Kernel

To create a simple console application that utilizes Semantic Kernel for AI processing, follow these development steps:

Step 1: Create a Console Application

Start by creating a new Console Application using Visual Studio:

  1. Open Visual Studio.
  2. Select "Create a new project".
  3. Choose "Console App (.NET)" and follow the prompts to set up your environment.

Step 2: Install Semantic Kernel Package

Open the NuGet Package Manager and search for Microsoft.SemanticKernel. Install the package into your project:

dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel
dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI

Step 3: Add Necessary Using Statements

In your Program.cs, add the following using statements:

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI;

Step 4: Set Up Your Azure OpenAI Credentials

Before diving into coding, make sure to have your Azure OpenAI credentials ready. You’ll need:

  • Your model deployment name
  • The endpoint URL
  • The API key (never expose this key in public repositories)

Based on what you scrape from the Azure AI Studio, ensure the endpoint is correct (it should not include unnecessary parameters).

Step 5: Create a Kernel Instance

Paste the following code snippet into your Main method to set up your kernel. Make sure to replace "your-model-endpoint" and "your-api-key" with your actual credentials.

var builder = Kernel.Builder();
const string deploymentName = "sk_test_deployment"; // Your deployment name
const string endpoint = "https://your-resource-name.azure.com"; // Trimmed endpoint
const string apiKey = "your-api-key"; // API Key

var kernel = builder
    .UseAzureOpenAI(endpoint, deploymentName, apiKey)
    .Build();

Step 6: Define the Summarization Function

Now that we have the kernel set up, define the function that will summarize a given text:

var prompt = "Given the following text, summarize it in one line:\n{input}";
var summarizeFunction = kernel.CreateFunction("summarize", prompt, new ExecutionSettings
{
    MaxTokens = 100, // Control the size of the output
    Temperature = 0.7 // Adjust it to make output more creative (0 to 1)
});

Step 7: Invoke the Summarization Function

Now, let’s summarize some text. Here's how you can do it:

var text1 = "Newton's laws of motion are three physical laws that together form the foundation for classical mechanics.";
var text2 = "The three laws of thermodynamics describe the relationships between heat, work, and energy.";

var summary1 = await kernel.InvokeAsync(summarizeFunction, new { input = text1 });
var summary2 = await kernel.InvokeAsync(summarizeFunction, new { input = text2 });

Console.WriteLine($"Summary 1: {summary1}");
Console.WriteLine($"Summary 2: {summary2}");

Complete Code Example

Here’s how your complete Program.cs might look:

using System;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI;

class Program
{
    static async Task Main(string[] args)
    {
        var builder = Kernel.Builder();
        const string deploymentName = "sk_test_deployment"; 
        const string endpoint = "https://your-resource-name.azure.com"; 
        const string apiKey = "your-api-key"; 
        
        var kernel = builder.UseAzureOpenAI(endpoint, deploymentName, apiKey).Build();

        var prompt = "Given the following text, summarize it in one line:\n{input}";
        var summarizeFunction = kernel.CreateFunction("summarize", prompt, new ExecutionSettings
        {
            MaxTokens = 100, 
            Temperature = 0.7 
        });

        var text1 = "Newton's laws of motion are three physical laws that together form the foundation for classical mechanics.";
        var summary1 = await kernel.InvokeAsync(summarizeFunction, new { input = text1 });

        Console.WriteLine($"Summary 1: {summary1}");
    }
}

Conclusion

Through this article, we’ve explored the incredible potential of Microsoft Semantic Kernel to empower applications with AI capabilities. With just a few simple steps, you can harness the power of natural language processing and intelligence in your applications. As you've seen, building simple AI applications with Semantic Kernel is straightforward, and the possibilities are expansive.

Tips for Further Exploration

  • Experiment with Prompts: Try different prompts to explore various functionalities (e.g., educational content generation, question answering).
  • File-based Prompts: In upcoming videos, we’ll look at how to read prompts from external files for more robust applications.
  • Adjust Execution Settings: Modify parameters like temperature or max tokens to customize outputs further.
  • Security Practices: Always secure your API keys and avoid exposing them in public repositories.

Stay tuned for more articles where we'll explore additional functionalities and more advanced AI integrations. Let’s continue to innovation in the world of AI!

Happy coding!

posts.title: Deep Dive into Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents Powered by AI Assistants - PART II
posts.html:
Welcome to the world of AI assistive technologies! In today’s blog post, we’ll explore how to leverage the Microsoft Semantic Kernel for creating AI-powered agents. This follows the latest insights from the YouTube video “Deep dive into Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents powered by AI Assistants” by Supreet.

Introduction

With the rise of AI-driven applications, understanding how to use tools like Microsoft's Semantic Kernel becomes vital. The Semantic Kernel allows developers to create intelligent agents that utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) through ‘semantic functions’ and ‘native functions’. In this guide, we will delve deeper into these concepts and walk through the creation of a simple application that generates jokes based on a user-defined topic.

Setting Up Your Development Environment

Before we dive into coding, ensure you have the necessary tools:

  1. .NET SDK installed (preferably .NET 5 or later)
  2. Visual Studio or any IDE of your choice
  3. An Azure account with access to the OpenAI services

Step 1: Create a New Console Application

To get started, open Visual Studio and create a new console application project called EscapeFromDemo.

Step 2: Install the Semantic Kernel NuGet Package

Navigate to the Tools menu, and from there go to NuGet Package Manager. Search for the Microsoft.SemanticKernel package and install it to your project.

Install-Package Microsoft.SemanticKernel
Install-Package Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI

Step 3: Configure Azure Settings

You will need your Azure configuration settings, which include:

  • Endpoint
  • Deployment Name
  • Model

Add these settings to your application. Below is a basic structure of what the setup should look like (ensure to fill in your actual data):

string endpoint = "YOUR_AZURE_ENDPOINT";
string deploymentName = "YOUR_DEPLOYMENT_NAME";
string apiKey = "YOUR_API_KEY";

Step 4: Initialize the Kernel

The next step is to initialize the Semantic Kernel builder and create the kernel instance:

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI;

// Create KernelBuilder
var builder = Kernel.Builder;
builder.WithAzureOpenAI(apiKey, endpoint, deploymentName);
var kernel = builder.Build();

Creating Semantic Functions

Semantic functions in the Semantic Kernel are the ones that utilize AI capabilities. Let’s create a joke generation function that uses AI to produce jokes based on a given topic.

Step 5: Setting Up Plugin Structure

  1. Create a folder named Plugins.
  2. Inside the Plugins folder, create a subfolder named FunPlugin.
  3. Create another folder inside FunPlugin named Joke.

In the Joke folder, create two files:

  1. SKPrompt.txt
  2. config.json

Step 6: Populate the Files

SKPrompt.txt (The prompt that will instruct the AI):

Write exactly one joke about a given topic. The joke must be G-rated, workplace, and family-safe, without any bias. 
Topic: {input}

config.json (Provides configuration for how the AI should execute):

{
  "$schema": "http://json.schemastore.org/semantickernel",
  "description": "Generate a funny joke.",
  "execution": {
    "maxTokens": 100,
    "temperature": 0.9
  },
  "parameters": {
    "input": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The subject for the joke.",
      "required": true
    },
    "style": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Optional hint for styling the joke.",
      "required": false
    }
  }
}

Step 7: Load Plugin and Invoke Function

Now, let’s load the plugin and invoke the function:

string pluginPath = Path.Combine(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory(), "Plugins/FunPlugin/Joke");

// Load the plugin
await kernel.ImportPluginFromPromptDirectory(pluginPath);

// Create arguments for the function
var args = new KernelArgument[]
{
    new KernelArgument("input", "Bollywood has lots of songs in the movies!"),
};

// Invoke the joke function
var result = await kernel.InvokeAsync("Joke", args);
Console.WriteLine(result);

Conclusion

In this article, we explored how to utilize the Microsoft Semantic Kernel to create simple AI-driven agents. We learned about semantic functions, how to structure plugins, and how to load and invoke functions defined in external text and JSON files.

Tips for Creating AI-Based Applications

  • Prompt Design: Spend time designing your prompts. Clear and concise prompts produce better results from AI models.
  • Configuration Management: Use configuration files to externalize your prompts and settings to keep your code clean.
  • Iterate and Experiment: Modify parameters like temperature and maxTokens to see how the output changes. Fine-tuning these can lead to better AI responses.

By following this guide, you can begin to harness the power of AI in your applications using Microsoft Semantic Kernel, opening up numerous opportunities in developer applications.

See you in the next exploration of advanced topics in AI! Happy coding!

posts.title: Building a Simple Chat Application with Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents - PART III
posts.html:
Welcome back to AI with Supreet! Today, we're embarking on an exciting journey as we create a basic chat application resembling ChatGPT using Microsoft's Semantic Kernel. If you have been following this series, you'll already be familiar with how we read prompts, create complex structures, and successfully implement plugins and functions using the Semantic Kernel. In this article, we will consolidate that knowledge and construct a minified chat application from scratch.

Introduction

The Semantic Kernel by Microsoft is a powerful framework designed to simplify the way we create and deploy AI models. With its elegant handling of prompts and execution settings, we can build conversational agents that can mimic human-like interactions. This blog post will guide you step-by-step through the process of building a fundamental chat application in C#.

Prerequisites

  • Basic understanding of C# and .NET.
  • Visual Studio or any preferred C# IDE installed.
  • .NET SDK installed.
  • An Azure account to access the Semantic Kernel services.

Getting Started

First, we need to create a new Console Application for our chat application and install the Semantic Kernel NuGet package.

dotnet new console -n SKChat
cd SKChat
dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel

Once your project is set up, open Program.cs and add the necessary using directives:

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Service;

Configuration

Now, let's set up our Semantic Kernel with the Azure endpoint, API key, and model name. For security reasons, it’s best to store these credentials in a configuration file or environment variables, but for simplicity, we’ll place them directly in the code.

var builder = KernelBuilder.Create();
builder.WithAzureTextCompletionService("<Your-EndPoint>", "<Your-API-Key>", "<Your-Model-Name>");
var kernel = builder.Build();

Make sure to replace <Your-EndPoint>, <Your-API-Key>, and <Your-Model-Name> with your actual Azure service details.

Creating a Chat Function

We will define a simple prompt for our chatbot. The chatbot will be able to respond to user inquiries in a conversational manner:

string prompt = "You are a chatbot that can have a conversation with users about any topic. You can provide explicit information where available or say 'I don't know' if you do not have an answer.";

Next, we'll create a Semantic Kernel function based on our prompt. This function will execute the logic of our chatbot.

var chatFunction = kernel.CreateFunctionFromPrompt(prompt, new FunctionExecutionSettings
{
    MaxTokens = 2000,
    Temperature = 0.7,
    TopP = 0.5
});

Implementing the Chat Loop

We will implement a simple loop to allow the user to chat with the bot continuously. For simplicity, let's create an infinite loop that prompts the user for questions until they decide to quit.

while (true)
{
    Console.WriteLine("I am a chatbot, ask me anything. Type 'exit' to quit.");
    string userInput = Console.ReadLine();
    
    if (userInput.Equals("exit", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        break;

    var result = await chatFunction.InvokeAsync(kernel, new KernelArgument(userInput));
    Console.WriteLine(result);
}

Make sure to run this code in an async environment; you may need to create an async Task Main to do so.

Adding Memory

Currently, our chatbot does not remember previous interactions, treating every inquiry as a new one. Let's add a simple memory feature by keeping track of chat history.

Modify the Prompt

We'll modify the prompt to include a history variable. The history will store prior interactions to provide continuity in conversations.

string history = string.Empty;

// Inside the chat loop
var fullPrompt = $"{history}\nUser: {userInput}\nChatbot: ";
var result = await chatFunction.InvokeAsync(kernel, new KernelArgument(fullPrompt));
history += $"User: {userInput}\nChatbot: {result}\n";

By appending the chat history after each response, our chatbot can recognize previous inputs.

Persisting Memory & Tokens Limitation

While this approach works for the current session, it poses two immediate challenges:

  1. Non-persistence: If the application is closed and restarted, history is lost.
  2. Token Limits: As conversations grow, we risk exceeding token limits set by the AI model.

Future Improvements

In our next session, we will explore persistent memory solutions and ways to optimize chat history to conform to token limits. Stay tuned for that!

Conclusion

Today, we took a significant step towards building a conversational agent by leveraging Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel. We learned how to set up the kernel, defined a prompt, created a chat function, and even managed a simple chat history.

As we continue refining our chat application, we will delve deeper into persisting user memory across sessions while optimizing our chat history.

Tips

  • Regularly refer to the Microsoft Documentation for updates on the Semantic Kernel.
  • Always secure your API keys and endpoints.
  • Experiment with different execution settings (Max Tokens, Temperature, TopP) to see how they affect responses.

If you found this tutorial helpful and are eager for more, please subscribe for updates on our next project, where we will enhance our chatbot's capabilities further. Until next time, happy coding!

# Example Code File
```csharp
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Services;
// Add any other necessary namespaces

class Program
{
    static async Task Main(string[] args)
    {
        var builder = KernelBuilder.Create();
        builder.WithAzureTextCompletionService("<Your-EndPoint>", "<Your-API-Key>", "<Your-Model-Name>");
        var kernel = builder.Build();

        string prompt = "You are a chatbot that can have a conversation with users about any topic. You can provide explicit information where available or say 'I don't know' if you do not have an answer.";
        var chatFunction = kernel.CreateFunctionFromPrompt(prompt, new FunctionExecutionSettings
        {
            MaxTokens = 2000,
            Temperature = 0.7,
            TopP = 0.5
        });

        string history = string.Empty;

        while (true)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("I am a chatbot, ask me anything. Type 'exit' to quit.");
            string userInput = Console.ReadLine();

            if (userInput.Equals("exit", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
                break;

            var fullPrompt = $"{history}\nUser: {userInput}\nChatbot: ";
            var result = await chatFunction.InvokeAsync(kernel, new KernelArgument(fullPrompt));
            history += $"User: {userInput}\nChatbot: {result}\n";
            Console.WriteLine(result);
        }
    }
}

This sample code encapsulates all the steps we've discussed, allowing you to build a base for your chat application. Happy coding!

posts.title: Deep Dive into Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents Powered by AI Assistants - PART IV
posts.html:
Introduction

The advent of artificial intelligence has transformed the way we build applications, particularly in the realm of natural language processing (NLP). Microsoft's Semantic Kernel is a powerful framework that allows developers to construct AI-powered agents capable of performing various tasks using natural language prompts. In this article, we will discuss how to work with prompts and configure them effectively within the Semantic Kernel framework. We will also explore essential parameters that govern the behavior of these AI models.

Understanding the Semantic Kernel Prompts

At the heart of any interaction with AI agents lies the prompt. A prompt acts as a blueprint that defines what task you want the AI model to perform. The Semantic Kernel allows you to manage prompts through an organized structure that includes reading from files and maintaining configuration settings.

Prompt Structure

When creating a prompt, you typically structure it with the following components:

  1. Name: The identifier for your prompt.
  2. Description: A brief summary of what the prompt does.
  3. Input Variables: The variables that act as input parameters for the task at hand.
  4. Execution Settings: Configurations that dictate how the model operates.

Here’s a simplified JSON representation of a prompt configuration:

{
  "name": "chat_assistant",
  "description": "A prompt for a chat assistant to provide responses based on user queries.",
  "input_variables": [
    "history",
    "request"
  ],
  "execution_settings": {
    "max_tokens": 150,
    "temperature": 0.7,
    "top_p": 0.9,
    "presence_penalty": 0.5,
    "frequency_penalty": 0.5
  }
}

Key Execution Settings Explained

After defining the structure of your prompt, you need to configure the execution settings. Each setting is vital in determining how the AI model processes inputs and generates outputs.

1. Max Tokens

Max tokens refer to the limit on how much text (in tokens) can be processed or generated. It's crucial to set this value according to the model's capabilities. For example, the default token limit for many models like GPT-3.5 is 4096 tokens.

2. Temperature

The temperature setting controls the creativity of the model's responses. Values range between 0 and 1:

  • Low values (0-0.3): Produce more deterministic, stable outputs.
  • Higher values (0.7-1): Generate more varied and creative responses.

3. Top-p (Nucleus Sampling)

This setting works in conjunction with temperature to refine generated outputs. If top_p is set to 0.9, the model will consider the top 90% of predicted tokens and sample from them. It allows for a more coherent response without straying into randomness.

4. Presence Penalty

This parameter ranges from -2 to 2 and penalizes tokens already present in the conversation history. A positive presence penalty encourages the model to introduce new ideas, enhancing the diversity of responses.

5. Frequency Penalty

posts.html:
In the world of artificial intelligence and chat applications, having a memory component can significantly enhance the user experience. In our previous video, we created a chat application that operated statelessly, meaning it didn't retain any information between sessions. Today, we’ll learn how to introduce a memory feature to our chat application using the Microsoft Semantic Kernel, specifically focusing on embedding and memory storage.

Introduction

The ability to store and recall information allows chat applications to provide interactive and personalized experiences. In this post, we'll dive into the concept of memory in chat applications, discuss embedding techniques, and showcase how to implement these in our Microsoft Semantic Kernel-based chat application.

Understanding Embeddings

Embeddings are mathematical representations of data that help in storing and retrieving information efficiently. Unlike traditional data storage methods, embeddings compress the information into a compact form while still preserving contextual relationships. This is particularly useful for chat applications where historical interaction data can quickly accumulate and take up space.

With embeddings, small chunks of input text can be converted into numerical representations (vectors) that are much smaller in size, making search operations faster and more efficient.

Getting Started

Before we jump into the code, ensure you have set up your environment correctly. You will need to install the following NuGet packages:

dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel
dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Memory.Core
dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Plugins.Memory --version <latest-pre-release>

Make sure to include the --version <latest-pre-release> for packages that do not have a stable release version available.

Setting Up the Application

First, let's set up our console application. We’ll add the necessary using directives for Semantic Kernel and Memory.

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Connectors.OpenAI;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Memory;

Configuration Parameters

You will also need to set up several configuration parameters, including an OpenAI API key and an Azure Embedding Endpoint.

var builder = new KernelBuilder()
    .WithAzureTextEmbeddingGeneration(
        new AzureTextEmbeddingGenerationConfig
        {
            Endpoint = "<Your-Azure-Endpoint>",
            ApiKey = "<Your-OpenAI-API-Key>",
            ModelName = "TextEmbeddingAda002" // Use a suitable embedding model
        });

Building the Chat Application

Start building the chat application based on our previous implementation. Initially, we'll create chat history without memory:

var chatPrompt = "You are a helpful assistant.";
var history = new List<string>();

while (true)
{
    Console.WriteLine("User: ");
    var userInput = Console.ReadLine();
    
    // Add user input to history and interact with AI
    history.Add(userInput);
    // Your logic for sending input to AI will go here
}

Adding Memory

Now, it’s time to add memory capabilities to our application. Follow these steps:

  1. Create a Memory Builder

    Initialize the memory builder and define how the memory will be stored.

    #pragma warning disable CS0618 // Suppress the warning for pre-release packages
var memoryBuilder = new MemoryBuilder(kernel);
var memory = memoryBuilder
    .UseOpenAITextEmbeddingGeneration("<Your-Azure-API-Key>")
    .UseMemoryStore(new VolatileMemoryStore())
    .Build();

  2. Updating the Chat Logic

    We’ll modify our chat logic to incorporate the memory object and handle fact retrieval.

    var chatFunction = kernel.GetFunction(chatPrompt);
var memoryParams = new MemoryCollectionParams(facts: new List<string> { "My name is Supreet." });

while (true)
{
    Console.WriteLine("User: ");
    var userInput = Console.ReadLine();
    
    var memoryResponse = memoryRecall.TryGetValue(userInput, out string recalledFact);
    if (memoryResponse)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"AI: I remember you saying: {recalledFact}");
    }
    
    history.Add(userInput);
    // Now include the memory in your prompts or functions as necessary
    // Pass 'memory' to your AI processing logic
}

Running the Application

Run your application, and the AI should now retain memory of information fed into it across sessions. Confirm that it remembers previous interactions and can respond based on those memories.

Testing

Test your setup with different inputs and check if the memory behaves as expected. For instance, ask your AI what your name is after you have told it, or ask it to recall facts about you.

Conclusion

With this implementation, we’ve effectively added a memory layer to our AI chat application using Microsoft Semantic Kernel. This allows our application to store user input efficiently while still performing well with minimal storage.

In future posts, we will explore persistent memory options, ensuring that our chat application can store and recall information even after restarts. We'll also look into the advanced capabilities of the kernel memory for more complex applications.

Tips for Development

  • Keep It Simple: Start with basic memory functionality before moving to more complex memory retrieval methods.
  • Test Regularly: Read through your AI's memory responses to check for accuracy and relevance.
  • Monitor Package Updates: Since we’re using pre-release packages, stay updated on any changes that may affect the stability of your application.

Happy coding! For further reading and updates, keep an eye on my blog: R Mauro.

This post is designed to be a comprehensive guide for developers looking to add memory features to their AI applications. Consider this a foundational step in creating more advanced AI functionalities using the Microsoft Semantic Kernel.

posts.title: Deep Dive Into Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents Powered by AI Assistants - PART VI
posts.html:
In the rapidly evolving world of artificial intelligence, the ability to efficiently manage complex tasks is crucial. One of the impressive advancements that aids in this effort is the concept of planners within Microsoft's Semantic Kernel. If you're looking to leverage AI in your production applications, understanding how to create and utilize planners can save considerable development time and improve efficiency.

Introduction

In a previous series of videos, we delved into how AI models respond to individual instructions, executing one prompt at a time. However, this method can lead to overwhelming complexity in production applications, especially as the number of prompts increases. This is where planners come into play, acting as orchestrators that streamline the handling of multiple tasks and function calls.

In this blog post, we will explore how to implement a planner using the Microsoft Semantic Kernel, allowing you to automate task management and coordination with AI assistants. We’ll walk through creating a console application that incorporates a planner to execute tasks in a way that minimizes manual function calls.

Development

Setting Up Your Project

Let’s begin our journey by creating a console application. We will be using the Semantic Kernel and its related NuGet packages, as follows:

  1. Create a new console application named xkplanner.
  2. Add the following NuGet packages:
    • Microsoft.SemanticKernel
    • Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Planning.Handlebars (note: this one is in pre-release).

Ensure your project file reflects these dependencies.

Code Structure

Add the necessary using statements at the top of your application:

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Planning.Handlebars;

Next, we’ll handle configuration settings for Azure services. Note that you’ll need to set your Azure configuration, which we will blur for privacy.

Creating the Planner

With the configuration in place, we can now start implementing the planner. Here’s the basic structure to create a planner in your application:

// Create a new Kernel Builder object
var kernelBuilder = new KernelBuilder()
    .WithAzureChatCompletion("<Azure-Config-Here>")
    .Build();

// Create a new Handlebars planner
var planner = new HandlebarsPlanner();

Next, we need to set up the plugins and their respective prompts. Let’s assume we have two plugins: summarize and short poem. You must create JSON configuration files for these plugins along with their respective prompt files, following these naming conventions:

  1. Plugin Folders

    • summarize_plugin
    • writer_plugin

  2. Prompt Files

    • sk_prompt.txt for summarizing
    • sk_prompt.txt for generating short poems

  3. Configuration Files

    • config.json for each plugin.

Here is a quick example of the configuration for the summarize plugin:

{
  "Description": "Summarize the given text",
  "ExecutionParameters": {
    "MaxTokens": 512,
    "Temperature": 0.0,
    "InputVariable": {
      "Name": "text",
      "Required": true
    }
  }
}

Your summarization prompt might look something like this:

Summarize the following input: {{text}}. Avoid using the following words: xxx, yyy, zzz.

For the short poem plugin, a possible configuration and prompt could be structured similarly, just with different text.

Once your plugins and prompts are in place, import them into the kernel:

// Import plugins to the kernel
await kernel.ImportPluginFromPromptAsync("summarize_plugin");
await kernel.ImportPluginFromPromptAsync("writer_plugin");

Creating and Executing Plans

After you have set up the plugins, it’s time to create your task request:

string ask = "Tomorrow is Valentine's Day. I need to come up with a few great ideas. My significant other likes poems, so write in the form of a poem.";
var originalPlan = await planner.CreatePlanAsync(kernel, ask);
Console.WriteLine("Original Plan: " + originalPlan);

You execute the created plan as follows:

var result = await originalPlan.InvokeAsync(kernel);
Console.WriteLine("Result: " + result);

Implementing Additional Skills

If you decide to enhance the planner with more skills, like writing a poem in the style of Shakespeare, you can create a new function and update your ask with the new plugin, subsequently generating a new plan and executing it.

string newAsk = "Valentine's Day is coming, and I need a date idea in the style of Shakespeare.";
var updatedPlan = await planner.CreatePlanAsync(kernel, newAsk);
var updatedResult = await updatedPlan.InvokeAsync(kernel);
Console.WriteLine("Updated Result: " + updatedResult);

Conclusion

Using planners in the Microsoft Semantic Kernel significantly reduces the burden of complex task management by streamlining multiple prompts and function calls into a cohesive workflow. This approach not only improves the efficiency of AI interactions but also helps in developing scalable applications that can adapt to various user requests.

Tips for Implementation

  • Organize Your Plugins: Maintain a clear and organized structure for your plugins and prompts to ensure smooth imports and avoid confusion.
  • Test Iteratively: Regularly test the execution of your plans after modifications to catch issues early.
  • Use Descriptive Names: Clear naming conventions for prompts and configuration files will help the planner identify tasks without ambiguity.
  • Explore Azure Capabilities: Don’t hesitate to dive deeper into Azure functionalities that can advance what your AI assistant can do.

With these insights and code samples, you should be well on your way to harnessing the power of planners in your own applications. Happy coding!

posts.title: Building RAG Applications with Microsoft Semantic Kernel and Kernel Memory - PART VII
posts.html:
Introduction

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Artificial Intelligence, one exciting development is the concept of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications. These apps enhance traditional AI models by combining the power of data retrieval with advanced text generation capabilities. In this article, we will delve into creating a simple RAG application using Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel and Kernel Memory, highlighting how you can build your applications in a few straightforward steps.

What Are RAG Applications?

RAG applications stand at the intersection of information retrieval and text generation. Essentially, they allow AI models to access a broad range of documents—be it PDFs, Word documents, web pages, or even videos—and retrieve specific content in response to user queries. This retrieval is followed by a generation phase, where the AI constructs coherent answers based on the retrieved material.

Overview of Kernel Memory

Kernel Memory is a powerful tool that simplifies the process of working with AI in RAG applications. Developed by Microsoft, it is built on the lessons learned from the earlier Semantic Memory and is designed to facilitate easier manipulation and querying of data from various sources. Using Kernel Memory allows developers to create RAG apps quickly—often in less than six steps!

Setting Up the RAG Application

Prerequisites

Before we dive into the coding part, ensure you have the following:

  • .NET SDK installed (version 6 or higher)
  • A valid OpenAI API key (you can get one from OpenAI's platform)

Step 1: Create a New Console Application

Open your terminal (or command prompt) and run:

dotnet new console -n RagApp
cd RagApp

Step 2: Install Required NuGet Packages

Inside your project directory, execute the following commands to install the necessary packages:

dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel --version 1.2.0
dotnet add package Microsoft.KernelMemory.Core --version 1.0.0
dotnet add package DotNetEnv --version 3.1.3

Step 3: Configure Environment Variables

Create a .env file in your project root to store your OpenAI API credentials. The contents of the file should resemble the following:

OpenAI_API_Key=your_api_key_here

Step 4: Implement the Core Application Logic

Now, open the Program.cs file in your solution and implement the following code:

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.KernelMemory.Core;
using DotNetEnv;
using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

namespace RagApp
{
    class Program
    {
        static async Task Main(string[] args)
        {
            // Load environment variables
            Env.Load();
            var apiKey = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("OpenAI_API_Key");

            // Initialize Kernel Memory
            var memory = new KernelMemoryBuilder().UseServerless(apiKey).Build();

            // Import a PDF document
            var documentId1 = "doc001";
            await memory.ImportDocumentAsync("path_to_your_pdf_document.pdf", documentId1);

            // Check if document processing is complete
            while (!await memory.IsDocumentReadyAsync(documentId1))
            {
                Console.WriteLine("Processing document...");
                await Task.Delay(1000);
            }
            Console.WriteLine("Document is ready!");

            // Chat with the memory
            while (true)
            {
                Console.Write("Ask a question: ");
                string question = Console.ReadLine();
                var answer = await memory.AskAsync(question, documentId1);
                Console.WriteLine($"Answer: {answer.Result}");
                Console.WriteLine($"Source: {answer.Source}");
            }
        }
    }
}

Note that you will need to replace path_to_your_pdf_document.pdf with the actual path to the PDF file you intend to use as a data source.

Step 5: Run Your Application

To run your application, use the command:

dotnet run

This will allow you to ask questions based on the content of your PDF document. The application retrieves the relevant information seamlessly from the provided document.

Step 6: Expanding the Application

You can also import data from web pages using a similar approach. For example, you can replace the import logic for documents with:

await memory.ImportWebPageAsync("https://example.com/your_web_page", "doc002");

This will enable the application to pull in data not only from files but also from online resources.

Conclusion

Creating RAG applications using Microsoft’s Semantic Kernel and Kernel Memory allows for easy integration of advanced AI capabilities into your projects. Within a few lines of code, you can transform how users interact with large sets of information, making it easy to retrieve and generate responses.

As you develop further, experiment with different data formats and explore deeper integrations to maximize the potential of RAG applications.

Tips for Development

  • Documentation is Key: Familiarize yourself with the official Semantic Kernel Documentation for more advanced features.
  • Test Your Limitations: Start with smaller documents initially, and gradually test with larger datasets.
  • Feedback Mechanisms: Implement logging and feedback within your application to ensure smooth performance and understanding model responses.

By following this guide, you will be well on your way to crafting effective and scalable RAG applications that leverage the best of AI capabilities. Happy coding!

posts.title: Deep Dive into Microsoft Semantic Kernel Agents Powered by AI Assistants - PART Final
posts.html:
Introduction

In the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence, the importance of integrating different types of functions into applications cannot be overstated. Microsoft Semantic Kernel (SK) stands out by allowing developers to harness the power of large language models (LLMs) alongside their custom code, referred to as "native functions." This blog post will explore how to leverage both semantic functions and native functions using SK to create versatile AI-driven applications. We’ll dive into a practical example that demonstrates this integration, ultimately creating a program that writes humorous weather-themed poems based on user input.

Understanding Semantic Functions and Native Functions

Semantic Functions

Semantic functions utilize the capabilities of an LLM to perform tasks such as generating text, summarizing information, or creating structured content based on prompts. For instance, if you needed a poem about a specific city, a semantic function would synthesize that based on language understanding and generation.

Native Functions

On the other hand, native functions refer to code that you write yourself. These functions perform tasks that are better handled via direct programming, such as API calls or data manipulations. An example might be fetching the weather by querying an external weather API with user-specific data.

The Application

In this example, we will create a console application that takes user input about visiting a city, retrieves the weather for that city using a native function, and finally generates a funny poem about what to wear, using a semantic function.

Development Steps

1. Create a New Console Application

Start by creating a new .NET Console Application and name it sk-native-functions. Make sure that you are using .NET 8 or later.

dotnet new console -n sk-native-functions
cd sk-native-functions

2. Install Required NuGet Packages

You will need to install the following NuGet packages:

  • Microsoft Semantic Kernel
  • Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Planners.Handlebars (Pre-release)
  • Newtonsoft.Json

You can install these packages using the following commands:

dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel --version 1.3.0
dotnet add package Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Planners.Handlebars --prerelease
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json

3. Set Up Classes and Structure

Create a Plugins folder in your project where you'll store both semantic and native functions. You'll need to define plugins such as CityDetectionPlugin and WeatherService.

a. Semantic Functions

Create a configuration JSON file and a C# function that exploits the LLM for city detection and composing a poem:

// findCity.json
{
  "description": "Extracts city name from user input.",
  "input_parameters": {
    "input": "The user input text."
  }
}

// writePoem.json
{
  "description": "Generates a humorous poem based on the city and weather.",
  "input_parameters": {
    "cityName": "The name of the city.",
    "weatherInput": "The weather details of the city."
  }
}

b. Native Functions

Create a C# class for city detection and another for weather fetching:

// CityDetectionPlugin.cs
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using System.ComponentModel;

public class CityDetectionPlugin
{
    [KernelFunction("getCityNameFromJson", Description = "Extracts city name from JSON input.")]
    public string GetCityNameFromJson(string jsonInput)
    {
        var jsonObject = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<dynamic>(jsonInput);
        return jsonObject?.city ?? "unknown";
    }
}

// WeatherService.cs
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

public class WeatherService
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;

    public WeatherService()
    {
        _httpClient = new HttpClient();
    }

    [KernelFunction("getWeatherAsync", Description = "Fetches weather data for the given city.")]
    public async Task<string> GetWeatherAsync(string city)
    {
        var response = await _httpClient.GetStringAsync($"https://api.weatherapi.com/v1/current.json?key=API_KEY&q={city}");
        return response; // Implement JSON parsing as needed.
    }
}

4. Implementing the Main Logic

In the Program.cs, import the plugins and create a planning mechanism for the AI to execute the functions appropriately.

using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Planners;
using Newtonsoft.Json;

// Create the kernel instance
var kernel = Kernel.Builder
    .WithOpenAI("YOUR_OPENAI_API_KEY")
    .Build();

// Load plugins
kernel.ImportPluginFromPromptDirectory("Plugins");

// Capture user input
Console.WriteLine("Please enter your travel message (e.g., 'I am visiting Seattle'):");
string userInput = Console.ReadLine();

// Create a new planner
var planner = new Planner(kernel);

// Plan execution
var plan = await planner.CreatePlanAsync("Generate a poem based on weather and city", userInput);
await plan.InvokeAsync();

5. Execute the Program

Now you can run the program and input a statement about visiting a city (e.g., "I am visiting Seattle"). The program will utilize both the native and semantic functions to determine the city name, fetch the weather, and generate a poem.

Conclusion

In summary, Microsoft Semantic Kernel brilliantly combines the prowess of AI with traditional programming through native and semantic functions. This dual capability allows developers to create rich, interactive applications that can perform complex tasks. With the example provided, we've illustrated how integrating native logic with AI prompts can create highly functional and engaging software solutions.

Tips for Implementation

  • Ensure that the descriptions for functions are clear to aid the planner's execution path.
  • Pay attention to how APIs handle errors, and consider implementing error-handling strategies in native functions.
  • Regularly update your NuGet packages to access the latest features and improvements.
  • Test various inputs to validate both semantic and native functionalities, ensuring they operate effectively together.

This combination of creativity and technology is at the forefront of AI advancement, and your journey with Microsoft Semantic Kernel can certainly lead to interesting and innovative applications. Happy coding!

posts.title: Building Your Own wc Tool in C# Code Challenge
posts.html:
The Unix wc (word count) tool is a classic command-line utility that counts the number of lines, words, and characters in a text file. In this post, we'll work on a minimalistic version of this tool using C#.

For this project let's focus on clarity over optimization, so even beginners can follow along.

Introduction

The wc tool is quite useful for analyzing text files in the terminal. It provides simple statistics:

  • Number of lines
  • Number of words
  • Number of characters
  • Number of bytes

This blog post is based on a code challenge where the goal is to recreate the functionality of the wc tool in your language of choice.

Below, we’ll build a minimal version of wc using C#.

Step-by-Step Implementation

First, let's break down what we'll need.

  1. Reading the file: We’ll use a stream to read the contents of the file.
  2. Counting lines, words, and characters: We'll write simple methods to count these.
  3. Handling command-line arguments: We'll add options to count specific things (lines, words, bytes, etc.).

Here’s the code for our minimal wc tool:

using System;
using System.IO;
using System.Linq;
using static System.Console;

if (args.Length == 0)
{
    PrintUsage();
    return;
}

var parsedArgs = ArgumentsParser.Parse(args);

try
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(parsedArgs.FilePath);
    long lineCount = 0, wordCount = 0, charCount = 0, byteCount = 0;

    string? line;
    while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) != null)
    {
        if (parsedArgs.CountLines) lineCount++;
        if (parsedArgs.CountCharacters) charCount += line.Length + 1; // +1 for newline character
        if (parsedArgs.CountWords) wordCount += CountWords(line);
        if (parsedArgs.CountBytes) byteCount += System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount(line) + 1;
    }

    if (parsedArgs.CountLines) Write($"{lineCount} ");
    if (parsedArgs.CountWords) Write($"{wordCount} ");
    if (parsedArgs.CountBytes) Write($"{byteCount} ");
    if (parsedArgs.CountCharacters) Write($"{charCount} ");
    WriteLine(parsedArgs.FilePath);
}
catch (FileNotFoundException)
{
    WriteLine($"Error: The file '{parsedArgs.FilePath}' does not exist.");
}

static long CountWords(string line)
{
    // Split the line by spaces and count non-empty entries
    var words = line.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
    return words.Length;
}

static void PrintUsage()
{
    const string usage_helper = @"Usage: ccwc [OPTION]... [FILE]...
  or:  ccwc [OPTION]... --files0-from=F
Print newline, word, and byte counts for each FILE, and a total line if
more than one FILE is specified.  A word is a non-zero-length sequence of
characters delimited by white space.

With no FILE, or when FILE is -, read standard input.

The options below may be used to select which counts are printed, always in
the following order: newline, word, character, byte, maximum line length.
  -c, --bytes            print the byte counts
  -m, --chars            print the character counts
  -l, --lines            print the newline counts
  -w, --words            print the word counts
      --help     display this help and exit
      --version  output version information and exit
      
!!!DISCLAIMER: This is a clone of famous wc (Word Count) command line. ";
    WriteLine(usage_helper);
}

A very simple ArgumentsParser.

public record class CWArgument(
    string FilePath, 
    bool CountBytes, 
    bool CountWords, 
    bool CountLines, 
    bool CountCharacters);

public static class ArgumentsParser
{
    /*
     * -c : number of bytes
     * -l : number of lines
     * -w : number of words
     * -m : number of characters
     * Default options - equivalent to -c -l -w
     */
    public static CWArgument Parse(string[] arguments)
    {
        var countB = arguments.Contains("-c") || arguments.Contains("--bytes");
        var countW = arguments.Contains("-w") || arguments.Contains("--words");
        var countL = arguments.Contains("-l") || arguments.Contains("--lines");
        var countM = arguments.Contains("-m") || arguments.Contains("--chars");
        var path = arguments[^1];

        var defaults = !countB && !countW && !countL && !countM;
        if (defaults) return new CWArgument(path, true, true, true, false);

        return new CWArgument(path, countB, countW, countL, countM);
    }
}

How It Works

  1. File Handling: We use a StreamReader to read the file line by line. This is the simplest way to handle file reading in C#.
  2. Counting Options: We handle the different counting options using the CWArgument record and the ArgumentsParser class. The parser processes the command-line arguments to determine what should be counted (bytes, words, lines, or characters). By default, it counts bytes, words, and lines, unless specified otherwise.
  3. Counting Lines, Words, and Characters: Depending on the options provided, we count the number of lines, words, characters, and bytes.
  4. Command-Line Arguments: The file path and options (e.g., -c for bytes) are passed as command-line arguments. The program parses them to determine which statistics to display.

Usage

To run the program, compile it and run it from the command line:

dotnet run -- -l -w -c <path_to_your_file>

For example:

dotnet run -- -l -w example.txt

The output will show the selected statistics based on the arguments passed. For example:

5 15 78 example.txt

This means the file example.txt has 5 lines, 15 words, and 78 characters.

Create an runnable executable

To do so all you need is.

dotnet publish -c Release -o ../output

Check the output folder recently created.

Special Mention

This implementation is a minimalist solution to the Build Your Own wc Tool challenge.

If you'd like to see a more refined version, including optimizations and additional features, check out my GitHub repository: Rmauro.CommandLines.WordCount.

Conclusion

We’ve built a minimalist version of the Unix wc tool in C# using just a few lines of code.

By adding argument parsing, we made the tool customizable based on the user’s needs.

This implementation is a great starting point for building command-line utilities and getting comfortable with file handling and argument parsing in C#.

You can experiment further by adding features or improving performance, but this version should give you a solid foundation.

Happy coding! 😎

posts.title: Socket Client over PowerShell
posts.html:
In this article let's use PowerShell to create a socket client and do a simple call to a webserver.

There are multiple ways to create sockets using PowerShell. For this article let's take use TcpClient object for it's simplicity.

Table of Contents

  • Set up the Client Socket
  • Sending the Request
  • Reading the Response
  • Closing the Connection
  • Complete Code

Set up the Client Socket

Let's start by creating the client object. TcpClient it's a very easy way to handle TCP connections as a client.

We're going to use the web server https://httpbin.org/ to connect our client.

# Creates the TCP Client
$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient

# Connect to the server
$client.Connect("eu.httpbin.org", 80)

Sending the Request

Since we're calling a Web Server HTTP 1.1. We must send the appropriate request as a HTTP 1.1 client.

# Data mimicking a web client
$payload = "GET /get HTTP/1.1
Host: eu.httpbin.org
Accept: */*

"

$bytesPayload = [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($payload) 
$stream.Write($bytesPayload, 0, $bytesPayload.Length)

Reading the Response

Once the request is sent we must immediately start reading the response.

# Receive data from the server
$bufferResponse = New-Object byte[] 4096 #enough to read our response 4mb
$bytesRead = $stream.Read($bufferResponse, 0, $bufferResponse.Length)
$response = [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($bytesRead, 0, $bytesRead)

# Output the Response
Write-Host $response

Finally! Close the connection

Don't forget to close the connection. 🚀

# Close the connection
$stream.Close()
$client.Close()

Complete Code

# Create a TCP client object
$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TcpClient

# Connect to the server
$client.Connect("eu.httpbin.org", 80) 

# Get the network stream for reading and writing
$stream = $client.GetStream() 

# Send data to the server
$data = "GET /get HTTP/1.1
Host: eu.httpbin.org
Accept: */*

"

$bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetBytes($data) 
$stream.Write($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)

# Receive data from the server
$buffer = New-Object byte[] 1024
$bytesRead = $stream.Read($buffer, 0, $buffer.Length)
$response = [System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($buffer, 0, $bytesRead)

# Display the response
Write-Host $response

# Close the connection
$stream.Close()
$client.Close()
